about: A sung note's vibrato: its measured numbers and the styles a singer sings it in, as configuration (public/shared/vocal/sung-vibrato.js reads all of it and holds none; the owner, 14 November 2026: "we use JSON and other standard configuration file formats to store all physical constants, configurable variables, and similar objects"; 16 November 2026: "Make sure the vibrato is wired in as per our configuration policy"). A style is added or changed here alone: a name, and either the `share` of the measured soloists' extent it sings, or the measured ensemble (`from`, its `sessions`) whose extents it takes; `afterSeconds`, how long into a note its vibrato begins, on a note whose stable stretch lasts `waitsFromSeconds` or more (every note where that is not given); and `wander`, the share of a singer's measured wander it sings (`wander`, below: what a held note's pitch does of itself, under any vibrato). `sung`: the style a singer of a written score takes where none is asked, by whether it sings alone or with others (native/vocaltract/sing-score.mjs).

sources.soloists: E. Prame (1997), "Vibrato extent and intonation in professional Western lyric singing", JASA 102, 616-621, doi:10.1121/1.419735, Table II: ten singers on commercial recordings of Schubert's Ave Maria, 25 tones each (seven women, three tenors); each row a singer's voice, its tones' mean extent and their largest and smallest, the standard deviation of its tones' extents between tones and (their mean) within a tone, cents centre to peak, and its mean rate, Hz.
sources.arch: Prame 1997, Fig. 5 (the mean over the tones, read from the figure): the extent, cents, of a tone's first eight cycles, and of its last eight, the last cycle's last.
sources.rate: E. Prame (1994), "Measurements of the vibrato rate of ten singers", JASA 96, 1979-1984, doi:10.1121/1.410141 (read in its preprint, STL-QPSR 33(4) (1992), 73-86): a tone's last `periods` quickening by `ratio` from the first of them to the last; the slowest and fastest single cycles, Hz; the range of the singers' standard deviations of their tones' rates, Hz.
sources.firstRising: D. Bell and M. Dobrovolsky (1999), "Acoustic characteristics of vibrato onset in singing", Proc. 14th ICPhS, San Francisco, 981-984: the share of five men's vibrato onsets whose first move is up.
sources.morphs: The measured soloists by morph: the tenors and the women, whose rates differ as three studies measured them (Prame's table 5.60 Hz against 6.13; Prame 1994 5.7 against 6.3; Shipp, Leanderson and Sundberg 1980, cited by Sundberg 1994, 5.4 against 5.9), their extents not.
sources.quartet: H. Daffern (2017), "Blend in singing ensemble performance: vibrato production in a vocal quartet", Journal of Voice 31(3), 385.e23-385.e29, doi:10.1016/j.jvoice.2016.09.007 (read in its accepted manuscript, White Rose eprint 108367; the trunk's research-downloads/voice/daffern-2017-vocal-quartet-vibrato): an SATB quartet of singers of 19 to 21, coached twice a week in ensemble singing and singing mostly Renaissance repertoire, recorded singing for blend by electrolaryngograph, each voice apart. Table 2, the row "Mean of all sung tones": each voice's mean extent, cents peak to peak, in her sessions 1, 2 and 4 (weeks 1, 3 and 9); 44 cents over all. The bass sang "very few tones" with vibrato; the alto's and tenor's long notes often a beat or two without it; the last, longest note of all three sessions "a non-vibrato tone for approximately one second before introducing vibrato", its extent growing to the tone's end.
sources.ours: The ensemble style takes the quartet's sessions once it was coached (2 and 4). Its wait: a second into a note whose stable stretch lasts two seconds or more, a shorter one's vibrato from its start (the owner, 16 November 2026, approving the correction: "yes, agreed; prepare the design that fixes these"; Daffern's soprano's one-beat notes "all contain vibrato, from close to the onset of the tone", her alto and tenor "withholding vibrato for the first two-beats" of their three-beat notes, and her last note straight "for approximately one second" -- until that evening the second was waited on every note, so that a shorter note was sung dead straight, which the owner heard as "a synthesizer-like vibrato"). One student quartet stands for ensemble singers until a professional ensemble's extents are read (research/SOURCES_TO_FETCH.md). The wander's: its standard deviation a singer's own, drawn about the mean of Ternström and Friberg's three vowels (10.8 cents) by their spread (3.5, pooled), never under `least`; its peak's frequency and Q each a singer's own, drawn evenly within their range (Q evenly in its logarithm), "under 1" taken as 0.5; the noise stepped at `rateHz`, the resonator Robert Bristow-Johnson's low-pass, started in its stationary state; the same for every vowel and pitch (their [a] wandered more than their [u]; their sopranos less than their basses, which they took for chance).
sources.wander: S. Ternström and A. Friberg (1989), "Analysis and simulation of small variations in the fundamental frequency of sustained vowels", STL-QPSR 30(3), 1-14 (the trunk's research-downloads/voice/ternstrom-friberg-1989): eight experienced choir singers -- two basses on D3, two tenors on A3, two altos on F#4, two sopranos on D5 -- each singing [u], [i] and [a] forte for about ten seconds "with as straight a tone as possible". Their F0's departure from its mean (their "flutter", wow included): its standard deviation by vowel, Table I, cents, mean and standard deviation over the tokens; its spectrum a peak between 4 and 6.5 Hz, from 0 to about 15 dB high, falling 6 to 12 dB an octave above it, each singer's own and the same over a singer's vowels; jitter always much smaller. Their model, "a simple second-order resonant low-pass circuit, to which a random 'white noise' signal is input", its resonance 4 to 6.5 Hz and its Q "from <1 to about 6": ten experienced listeners could not tell its contours from the singers' own.
